newsitem.title: UK: Billiton wins instant blue chip status in UK.
newsitem.headline: Billiton wins instant blue chip status in UK.

text.p: South African base metals group Billiton Plc on Tuesday gained instant blue chip status on the London stock market after successfully placing 375 million new shares here.
Amid strong interest from both British and overseas investors, Billiton's new shares were placed at 220 pence, which was well within the 210-240 range set earlier by Gencor.
The shares opened at an 8-1/2 pence premium to the placing price but later retreated to 221-1/2 pence in late morning dealings amid bearish comment from analysts.
The placing is part of the group's demerger from mining house Gencor Ltd , which will focus on its precious metals operations while Billiton seeks to expand beyond its home base.
With a total market capitalisation of some 4.6 billion pounds ($7.7 billion), Billiton is the 56th biggest London-listed company, meaning it will enter the FTSE 100 index at the next review.
Billiton said its London listing would give it extra financial muscle to take advantage of opportunities as they arose around the world.
No longer hampered by South African exchange controls, Billiton wants to expand existing operations while also eyeing privatisation projects in countries such as Venezuela, Colombia and Brazil.
"We are delighted by the strong levels of support from international investors and welcome our new shareholders," Billiton chairman Brian Gilbertson said.

Billiton shares were among the most actively traded on the London Stock Exchange as more than 13 million shares changed hands less than four hours after trading started on a "conditional" basis, meaning before formal allocation of shares.
Calculating Billiton's net asset value at less than 200 pence per share, analyst James Leahy at T. Hoare & Co said: "The shares are fully priced and on this valuation they offer limited upside."

Leahy added he could see no reason why Billiton -- although considered a very well run group -- should trade at a premium to net asset value while other mining groups were valued at discounts of up to 30 percent.
Paribas Capital Markets analyst Emile Morfett said Billiton shares were probably supported by strong demand from funds obliged to invest in FTSE 100 stocks.
But he too considered Billiton overvalued, pointing to political and currency risks stemming from Billiton's mainly South African asset base.
"Given the South African exposure, Billiton is at a premium to Rio Tinto and I think the shares are at least 10 percent overvalued," Morfett said.
Anglo-Australian Rio Tinto -- the only other FTSE 100 mining stock -- eased three pence to trade at 1,002-1/2. ($ = 0.597 British Pounds)
